questions.question_text: A presentation is:
options: A structured delivery of information to an audience, usually with visual aids, to inform, persuade or train
questions.explanation: Its purposes include informing, persuading, motivating and training.

questions.question_text: The first step in planning a presentation is to:
options: Define the purpose and analyse the audience
questions.explanation: Then organise content, design visuals and rehearse.

questions.question_text: Audience analysis is important because:
options: It lets you tailor content, language and examples to their needs and knowledge

questions.question_text: The purpose and objectives of a presentation should be defined as:
options: Clear, specific and measurable statements of what you want the audience to know, feel or do

questions.question_text: Content should be organised:
options: Logically with a clear opening, body and closing, with key points in order

questions.question_text: The rule of three in presentations means:
options: People remember ideas best in groups of three, so structure key points in threes
questions.explanation: E.g., "tell them what you'll say, say it, summarise."

questions.question_text: A common guideline for slide timing is:
options: About one to two minutes per slide

questions.question_text: A common division of time is:
questions.explanation: The body gets most of the time.

questions.question_text: A project presentation is:
options: A presentation of the work, findings and conclusions of a project, e.g., a survey on digital payments
questions.explanation: It is common in academic and business settings.

questions.question_text: The standard structure of a presentation is:
questions.explanation: Opening introduces, body develops, closing summarises.

questions.question_text: Elements of a good opening include:
options: A greeting, hook, introduction of self and topic, objective and agenda

questions.question_text: Ways to begin a presentation include:
options: A question, a story, a statistic, a quotation or a bold statement

questions.question_text: A hook is:
options: An attention-grabbing opening, e.g., "Did you know 9 out of 10 online frauds start with a link?"
questions.explanation: It makes the audience want to listen.

questions.question_text: An agenda slide:
options: Outlines the topics that will be covered in the presentation
questions.explanation: It helps the audience follow the structure.

questions.question_text: The body of a presentation should include:
options: Key points supported by evidence, examples and visuals in logical order
questions.explanation: Keep it focused on the objectives.

questions.question_text: Transitions are:
options: Words or phrases that link ideas or sections, e.g., "Moving on to…", "Next…", "In contrast…", "As a result…", "To summarise…"

questions.question_text: A presentation should be concluded by:
options: Summarising key points, restating the main message and ending with a call to action or strong closing

questions.question_text: A call to action is:
options: A request that tells the audience what to do next, e.g., "Start a SIP today."

questions.question_text: A suitable slide-by-slide outline for "Analysing UPI Adoption among College Students" is:
options: Title; objectives; methodology; findings; analysis; conclusion and recommendations; references
questions.explanation: It follows a standard project format.

questions.question_text: A suitable outline for "Customer Satisfaction in Online Banking" includes:
options: Title, objectives, survey method, satisfaction findings, issues, recommendations and conclusion

questions.question_text: A suitable outline for "A Business Plan for a Campus Café" includes:
options: Idea, market, product/menu, costs, revenue projection, marketing and conclusion
questions.explanation: It follows a business plan structure.

questions.question_text: A suitable outline for "Impact of Social Media on Buying Behaviour" includes:
options: Introduction, objectives, research method, findings, discussion and recommendations

questions.question_text: A suitable outline for "Feasibility of an Electric Scooter Rental Start-up" includes:
options: Problem, market analysis, financials, risks, feasibility conclusion

questions.question_text: A good introduction for "Financial literacy among youth" is:
options: "Good morning. Today I will show why understanding money early shapes a young person's future."

questions.question_text: A good closing for "Financial literacy among youth" is:
options: "In short, financial literacy builds confident young adults; start learning today."

questions.question_text: A good hook for a presentation on "Cybersecurity in banking" is:
options: "Every minute, someone loses money to an online banking scam. Could it be you?"

questions.question_text: Good objectives for "Mutual funds: awareness among students" are:
options: "To measure students' awareness of mutual funds, identify barriers and recommend ways to improve literacy."

questions.question_text: A methodology slide for a survey on digital payments should state:
options: The sample size, sampling method, tools (questionnaire) and period
questions.explanation: It explains how data was collected.

questions.question_text: The best findings slide for "92% use UPI daily, 60% fear fraud, 45% use cashback offers" is:
options: A bar chart or concise bullets: UPI daily 92%, fear fraud 60%, cashback 45%

questions.question_text: A good conclusion and recommendations slide for the UPI project states:
options: Key findings and actions, e.g., "Raise fraud awareness and promote safe UPI practices."

questions.question_text: Principles of effective slide design include:
options: Simplicity, readability, consistency and visual hierarchy

questions.question_text: The 6×6 rule says:
options: No more than six bullets per slide and six words per bullet

questions.question_text: The 10-20-30 rule (Guy Kawasaki) says:
options: 10 slides, 20 minutes and a font of at least 30 points
questions.explanation: It keeps presentations short and readable.

questions.question_text: Recommended font sizes are:
options: Titles around 32–44 pt and body text about 24–28 pt
questions.explanation: Large enough for the back row.

questions.question_text: When choosing colours, one should:
options: Use high contrast, limit the palette and avoid red-green combinations for colour-blind viewers

questions.question_text: The right chart: bar for _____, line for _____, and pie for _____:
options: Parts of a whole; time; categories
Comparing categories; trends over time; parts of a whole
questions.explanation: Use pie charts only for few categories.

questions.question_text: The best slide version of "Our survey of 100 students found that most use UPI daily because of convenience, though some worry about fraud" is:
options: The full sentence in tiny font
Title: UPI Usage (n = 100); bullets: most use UPI daily; reason: convenience; concern: fraud

questions.question_text: Common mistakes in slide design include:
options: Too much text, small fonts, poor contrast and distracting animations

questions.question_text: Visual aids other than slides include:
options: Handouts, charts, models, flip charts and videos
questions.explanation: Choose the aid that suits the audience.

questions.question_text: Animations and transitions should be used:
options: Sparingly, to support understanding not distract

questions.question_text: Presentation tools include:
options: PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva and Keynote
questions.explanation: Choose one suited to your needs.

questions.question_text: Presenter view and speaker notes allow:
options: The speaker to see notes, the next slide and a timer while the audience sees only the slide

questions.question_text: To make a presentation accessible, one should:
options: Use alt text, readable fonts, high contrast and captions

questions.question_text: On slides, sources are cited by:
options: Adding a short source line (author, year) and a full references slide

questions.question_text: Copyright issues with images arise when:
options: Images are used without permission or licence; use royalty-free or credited images

questions.question_text: Verbal delivery skills include:
options: Clear voice, appropriate pace, volume, pauses and emphasis

questions.question_text: Non-verbal delivery skills include:
options: Posture, gestures, facial expressions and eye contact

questions.question_text: Eye contact during a presentation should be:
options: Spread across the audience, holding each person for a few seconds

questions.question_text: Gestures should be:
Nervousness is caused by fear of judgement, lack of preparation and inexperience, and can be controlled by:
options: Preparation, practice, deep breathing and positive visualisation

questions.question_text: Ways to engage the audience include:
options: Questions, polls, stories, examples and eye contact

questions.question_text: One should not read directly from the slides because it:
options: Bores the audience and makes you seem unprepared
questions.explanation: Slides are visual aids, not scripts.

questions.question_text: To rehearse a presentation, one should:
options: Practise aloud, time it, and get feedback

questions.question_text: To manage time during a presentation, one should:
options: Rehearse with a timer, keep key points flexible and watch the clock

questions.question_text: When technology fails, one should:
options: Stay calm and continue with backups such as printed notes or handouts

questions.question_text: Backups to keep include:
options: A copy on a pen drive and in the cloud, a PDF version and printed notes

questions.question_text: A group presentation is:
options: A presentation delivered by a team, with each member presenting part of the content

questions.question_text: Roles within a group presentation include:
options: Introducer, content presenters, tech handler and Q&A closer

questions.question_text: In a group presentation, content should be divided:
options: According to strengths and logical sections with equal contribution

questions.question_text: A smooth hand-over between team members includes:
options: A linking sentence such as "Now my colleague Riya will explain the findings."

questions.question_text: A do of group presentations is:
options: Rehearse together and keep to time limits
questions.explanation: A don't is to contradict teammates.

questions.question_text: When not speaking, team members should:
options: Stand attentively and support the speaker

questions.question_text: To prepare for the Q&A session, one should:
options: Anticipate likely questions and prepare answers

questions.question_text: When you cannot answer a question, you should:
options: Admit it honestly and offer to find out later

questions.question_text: To handle a hostile question:
options: Stay calm, acknowledge the concern and answer factually

questions.question_text: You should repeat or paraphrase a question because it:
options: Ensures everyone heard and gives you time to think

questions.question_text: A Q&A session is closed by:
options: Thanking the audience and summarising the key message

questions.question_text: Common questions after a project presentation include:
options: Sample size, methodology, limitations and recommendations

questions.question_text: Evaluation criteria of a presentation include:
options: Content, structure, delivery, visuals, timing and Q&A handling

questions.question_text: A rubric for a project presentation would typically include:
options: Criteria such as content, organisation, delivery, visuals and teamwork, with score levels

questions.question_text: Peer evaluation is:
options: Assessment of a presentation by classmates using given criteria

questions.question_text: Feedback improves presentation skills by:
options: Identifying strengths and areas for improvement
questions.explanation: Act on it in the next presentation.

questions.question_text: Plagiarism in presentations is:
options: Using others' content, images or ideas without credit

questions.question_text: Ethical considerations for survey data include:
options: Consent, confidentiality, honesty in reporting and no manipulation

questions.question_text: A presentation checklist includes:
options: Objective, content, visuals, rehearsal, equipment check and backups

questions.question_text: For a presentation, one should dress:
options: Neatly and professionally as per the occasion

questions.question_text: Storytelling makes a presentation more effective by:
options: Making points memorable and emotionally engaging

questions.question_text: A data story is:
options: A narrative that explains data with context, visuals and a message

questions.question_text: To present statistics to a non-technical audience, one should:
options: Use simple language, round numbers, visuals and analogies

questions.question_text: A five-minute business pitch usually covers:
options: Problem, solution, market, business model, team and ask

questions.question_text: To adapt a presentation to a virtual audience, one should:
options: Keep slides simple, engage often and test the technology

questions.question_text: Polls such as Mentimeter are used to:
options: Engage the audience by collecting live responses

questions.question_text: A best practice of online presentations is:
options: Check audio and video, use a clear background and keep the audience engaged

questions.question_text: A good 2-minute self-introduction for a team presentation includes:
options: Name, role, a key fact and the topic you will cover

questions.question_text: A smooth hand-over script is:
options: "That covers the findings; now my teammate will present the recommendations."

questions.question_text: To present a failure honestly, one should:
options: State what happened, lessons learnt and next steps

questions.question_text: To handle a time overrun:
options: Skip less important points and move to the conclusion

questions.question_text: A strong closing line is:
options: "Remember: small savings today build big security tomorrow."
questions.explanation: It is memorable and ties to the message.

questions.question_text: When presenting a pitch to investors, one should highlight:
options: The problem, solution, market size, traction, financials and the ask

questions.question_text: An agenda slide for a project on mutual funds would list:
To present survey results with a bar chart, you:
options: Use a table of raw data
Plot categories on one axis and percentages on the other, with a clear title and labels, e.g., UPI 92%, fear fraud 60%

questions.question_text: A title slide contains:
options: The topic, presenter's name, date and institution

questions.question_text: A references slide lists:
options: All sources used in a consistent citation style, e.g., author, year, title

questions.question_text: A presentation differs from a speech in that a presentation:
options: Uses visual aids and structured content, while a speech relies mainly on words

questions.question_text: To make a presentation persuasive, one should:
options: Know the audience, use ethos, pathos and logos, and end with a call to action

questions.question_text: To explain a complex idea simply, one should:
options: Use analogies, examples and visuals and avoid jargon

questions.question_text: A storyboard in presentation design is:
options: A sketch or plan of the slides and flow before creating them

questions.question_text: To conclude a presentation on a failed project, one should:
options: Summarise lessons learnt and recommendations for the future

questions.question_text: What makes a presentation memorable is:
options: A clear message, stories, strong visuals and a confident delivery

questions.question_text: Qualities of a good presenter include:
options: Confidence, clarity, preparation and audience engagement
